title: The summit
hookLine: five years of stories, practices, texts, saints and silence, and the path goes on in eternity
tomorrow: what's the first step on the other side of the summit?
last: I BELIEVE · I HOPE · I LOVE.

lines: THE PHOTO, THE SNACK, THE VIEW.
I HAVE LIFTED UP MY EYES.
cards: Hikers will tell you the summit is a strange place. You take the photo, eat something, look at how small the parking lot is.
And then, sooner than you'd like, you have to decide what's next, because nobody lives on a peak. So: you reach the top. Now what?

The question is older than hiking. A psalm the Church prays puts it like this, in the Douay-Rheims: "I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from whence help shall come to me." The mountain isn't the point.
It's where you look up from.

teach.b: Look back down the mountain for a moment: stories, practices, the texts read in their own words, saints from every century, and a lot of silence.
Paul has a word for what comes next, in the Douay-Rheims: "forgetting the things that are behind, and stretching forth myself to those that are before, I press towards the mark."
Not forgetting as erasing; forgetting as not stopping.

teach.h: NO EDGE TO GOD, NO END TO SEEKING.
teach.b: Gregory of Nyssa, an early Church Father, took the same idea further: for him, the one who seeks God never reaches an end to seeking, because God has no edge.
And Paul again: "Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard," what God has prepared for those who love him. Catholics believe the path goes on past this life, into eternity. Now a neighbor.

teach.h: THE LAST LINE, THEN IN THE BEGINNING.
teach.b: When a congregation finishes reading the Torah, Jewish tradition has them read the last lines of Deuteronomy and then, that same day, begin again: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth."
And at the end of each book, the room calls out chazak, chazak, venitchazek: be strong, be strong, and let us be strengthened.
Shared ground: an ending that turns, right away, into a beginning.
The honest difference: for Jews the circle of Torah begins again, here, together; for Catholics the summit points beyond this world, toward a God the eye hasn't seen. Two ways of not stopping.
Here's one to tell a friend tonight: some traditions end their holy book by opening it again.

how: Catholics speak of the Christian life as a pilgrimage that continues into eternity; at the end of a retreat or a season of prayer, many simply begin the daily round of prayer again.

o: the top of the path: look back, give thanks, go on
the finish line, where the climbing finally stops
a sign of having become better than others

games.q: the view from the top — tap the pairs.
p: I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains

s: for Catholics, reaching the end of a path means you've arrived
Paul presses on, and the Church speaks of the path going on into eternity.
Jewish tradition finishes the Torah and starts Genesis again the same day
the last lines of Deuteronomy, then "In the beginning".
Jewish and Catholic ideas of what comes after the summit are the same
they share an ending that turns into a beginning; Jews begin the Torah again, Catholics look toward eternity.

games.q: you've just finished something huge: a degree, a season, a five-year path. the next morning feels flat. on today's lesson, what's the move?
o: look back, give thanks, and take the next small step.
rest for good; you earned the right to stop.
start something bigger right away so it doesn't end.
games.why: Paul forgets what's behind by not stopping, and stretches forth. the summit is where you look back, give thanks, and keep walking.

practice: Stand up and stand still. Turn your head and look back over your shoulder, and name one thing from this whole climb you're thankful for. Then face forward and take a few slow steps, as if onto a new trail.
If you pray, you can lift your eyes the way the psalm does, and say thank you.

wordCard.voice: The summit. Not the end of the path, but the place you look back, give thanks, and keep walking.

orig.note: Latin: I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains. the Vulgate's Psalm 120 (121).

carryVoice: The last line to keep: the summit is a beginning, five years up and the path still going. Keep walking.
